newsitem.title: UK: Argentina sees unemployment falling on high growth.
newsitem.headline: Argentina sees unemployment falling on high growth.

text.p: Argentina's economy minister on Tuesday predicted high unemployment would fall as the economy recovered and said attacks by trade union leaders on proposed labour reforms were due their fear of losing power.
In an interview with Reuters, Roque Fernandez also shrugged off accusations by his outspoken predecessor of rampant official corruption, saying the problem had already largely been solved.
"We believe that unemployment figures are going to be significantly reduced in the first semester of 1997 because industrial output...is growing at a very rapid pace," he said.
Fernandez is in London at the head of a 100-strong economic mission, by far the largest from Argentina since the 1982 Falklands War.
Recession, from which Argentina is only just starting to emerge, has seen unemployment surge to around 17 percent, accompanied by harsh fiscal measures and plans to free up the labour market.
Fernandez noted that industrial output was now growing at around an annual 10 percent.
Argentina's top union leader on Monday warned that the ruling party would lose legislative elections next year unless it scrapped austerity measures and eased up on planned labour reforms.
"The government wants to introduce some modifications to the labour legisation especially to promote the creation of new jobs," Fernandez said.
"Of course, there is a struggle or competition for power and the labour union leaders wouldn't like to lose the power they have. That probably explains their criticism...of the government," he said.
He repeated his growth forecast for next year of five percent, but added it was a conservative prediction.
For every three percentage points rise in gdp, unemployment will fall one point, he said.

Commenting on the outspoken criticisms of the way the government operates by former economy minister Domingo Cavallo, whom he replaced earlier this year, Fernandez said there was no impact on the economy.
"We may have this sort of political competition without affecting the economy in any siginifcant way," he said.
On Cavallo's charges of widespread corruption, Fernandez said the problem was disappearing.

"Corruption in Argentina has been fought in a very signficant way because most of it was in the public enterprises which were privatised. Some of the corruption that may be left is in the customs, which we are privatising," he said.
